Chapter 7. The Wisdom of Letting Go.
Letting go—now, that’s one of those ideas that sounds so simple, but when you’re in the thick of things, it can feel nearly impossible, right? When you’ve been hurt or misunderstood, your mind just grabs onto the story and won’t let go. It’s like it keeps hitting replay, over and over. The urge to hold on—whether it’s to anger, blame, or that deep need for justice—can be absolutely overwhelming.
There’s this man I once heard about. He carried a heavy resentment toward a colleague who’d taken credit for his work. For months, he replayed that moment in his head, fueling his anger every single time. It got to the point where the resentment became his constant companion—it colored all his interactions and just drained his energy day after day.
One night, after tossing and turning, he realized something important: holding on was actually hurting him far more than anyone else. So, he decided to try letting go. Not by pretending it didn’t matter—but by really acknowledging the pain, and then choosing not to feed it anymore. He wrote down what he felt, talked it out with a friend he trusted, and then, with a deep breath, just set the story aside.
The relief he felt was immediate—even if it wasn’t perfect. Sure, that resentment popped back up now and then, but each time, he gently reminded himself, “I can notice this. I don’t have to hold on.” And over weeks and months, the grip of that old story started to loosen. He found himself more at ease, more able to focus on what truly mattered.
Letting go doesn’t mean you forget, or excuse the harm that was done. Here’s something to pay attention to—it’s about releasing the need to keep the wound alive. Most people don’t realize, forgiveness isn’t really a gift for the other person—it’s something you give yourself. It’s a way to get your energy back, to reclaim your attention, and to make space for healing.
There was also a mother who struggled for years to let go of anger toward her own parents. Those old hurts ran deep, and the urge to blame never seemed to go away. But through gentle reflection and a little self-compassion, she started to see her parents as people—with their own struggles and limitations. The anger began to soften. It was replaced by a sense of understanding. She didn’t excuse what they’d done, but she no longer let it define her.
Letting go—it’s not just a moment, it’s a practice. It takes patience, honesty, and a willingness to come back, again and again, to the present moment. Each time you choose to release a bit of that old story, you make more space for what’s possible—peace, connection, even a little joy.
